#### Learning Objectives

* Understand the aim and design of a typical correlation profiling subcellular proteomics experiment
* Understand De Duve's principle
* Understand the the use-case DIA-LOP subcellular proteomics experiment
* Understand what DIA-NN does and what data it outputs for downstream analysis

## Subcellular proteomics

The field of subcellular spatial proteomics is centered on the determination of
protein localisation within the cell. Importantly, protein localisation is
intimately linked to protein function and is vital for research into basic
biological mechanisms impacting the health and disease of all organisms [@Sigaeva2026].

Quantitative mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics methods have been developed
to study protein localisation at the proteome-wide level and generate
subcellular "maps". Several high throughput MS-based correlation profiling
methods have been established and include the Localisation of Organelle Proteins
(LOP) family of methods [@Sadowski2006; @Geladaki2019; @Christoforou2016;
@Kieran2025], dynamic organellar maps (DOMs) [@Itzhak2016], protein correlation
profiling (PCP) [@Foster2006], sequential detergent-based solubilisation
[@MartinezVal2021], COLA [@Mardakheh2017], Prolocate [@Jadot2017] and
SubcellBarCode [@Orre2019]. Despite subtle differences in experimental design, 
as summarised in the figure below, all of these methods generate a similar data 
matrix (PSM, peptide or protein abundance across fractions) and can be analysed 
using the same subcellular proteomics software. 

Generation of correlation profiling data requires considerable effort,
expense and well thought-out experimental designs for successful implementation.
Equally, data analysis involves considerable time and investment to produce high
quality, robust datasets which enable meaningful biological interpretation and
utility to the research community.

In this course material, we provide an updated workflow for the processing and
analysis of correlation profiling-based spatial proteomics data, based on our
F1000 workflow [@Hutchings2025]. We cover the key steps required to extract
spatial information from quantitative correlation profiling MS data. The first
step requires data importation, processing, and quality control followed by the
definition of subcellular markers. We discuss how to curate such markers using
approaches including unsupervised clustering and dimensionality reduction. Next,
we show how to use subcellular markers to generate spatial proteome maps. This
involves the classification of protein localisation through classical or
Bayesian semi-supervised machine learning algorithms using the [`pRoloc`
package](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/pRoloc.html).

## Software

In this workflow we use R packages from Bioconductor, namely, the
[`QFeatures` package](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/QFeatures.html)
for upstream data processing and the [`pRoloc`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/pRoloc.html) for downstream 
machine learning.

## MSnSets versus QFeatures data structures
In our first [F1000 workflow for spatial proteomics](https://f1000research.com/articles/5-2926) 
[@Breckels2018] we used the [`MSnbase` package](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/MSnbase.html) 
and the `MSnSet` infrastructure for storing and manipulating our spatial
proteomics data. In this workflow, we have transitioned to working with the 
`QFeatures` package for data processing. Whilst `MSnbase` provides functionality 
for manipulating and storing quantitative proteomics data, the `QFeatures` 
infrastructure makes it possible to store all levels of the data together in one 
object with explicit links maintained between hierarchical levels. For example,
it is possible to store the peptide spectrum matches (PSMs), peptides and proteins
(among other types of data) derived from all replicates of an experiment together,
in one single data container. 
:::

## The use-case: Subcellular mapping of U-2 OS cells

As a use-case, we will analyse a label-free DIA subcellular proteomics dataset
from a partially differentiated human osteosarcoma (OS) cell line (U-2 OS cells)
[@Kieran2025]. U-2 OS cells are one of the earliest described cancer derived cell lines
and have been applied across many areas of research. For subcellular proteomics they have
been widely used in benchmarking as they provide a robust, flat, epithelial-like
morphology and a deeply profiled human proteomic reference map.

Mass spectrometry (MS)-based protein correlation profiling data can be generated
using a number of methodologies. These methods can differ with respect to (1)
biochemical fractionation, (2) peptide quantitation (label-based or label-free),
and (3) mass spectrometry acquisition method (data-dependent acquisition, DDA,
or data-independent acquisition, DIA).

Our use-case data was generated using the DIA-LOP method from the Lilley lab at
the Universisty of Cambridge. DIA-LOP (Data-Independent Acquisition
Localization of Organelle Proteins) is a high throughput subcellular
proteomics method that offers a faster, label-free, and cost-effective
alternative to classic multiplexed LOPIT methods [@Kieran2025]. The pipeline works by gently
lysing cells and using differential ultracentrifugation to separate intact
organelles into 10 distinct fractions based on density. Instead of using
expensive chemical tags e.g. tandem mass tags (TMT), these fractions undergo
label-free peptide digestion and are analyzed via advanced DIA mass
spectrometry, which systematically fragments all ions to capture low-abundance
proteins from very low sample inputs. For each fraction, a total of 750 ng of peptide
was analysed using using a timsTOF HT mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, 
Germany) coupled with a nanoElute 2 UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics). 

For the paper, the data was processed using the freely available
[DIA-NN](https://github.com/vdemichev/DiaNN) software (v 1.8.2 beta 27) [@Demichev2019] 
for peptide and protein identification and quantification, followed by the
Bioconductor
[QFeatures](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/QFeatures.html)
package to aggregate and process precursor-level data into robust protein
abundance profiles. Subsequently, the
[pRoloc](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/pRoloc.html)
package was used for protein subcellular localisation and the generation of
subcellular maps, matching the abundance profiles of unknown proteins against
known organelle markers to map over 8,000 protein groups across 13 subcellular
compartments. The raw MS data is available online through ProteomeXchange via
the PRIDE repository under the identifier [PXD063082](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/archive/projects/PXD063082).

## Identification search of the raw MS data
Database searching of MS data involves comparing the observed MS spectra
to expected MS spectra generated via in silico digestion of a selected protein 
database. Since the use-case data used human cells, we provided the SwissProt 
human proteome to DIA-NN as the database for searching. We also provided a 
database of common contaminants that could be present in our sample due to (i)
human contamination (e.g., keratin from nails, hair or skin), or (ii) sample
preparation (e.g., enzymes used for protein digestion). These two databases are
can be found in the course materials and also
[here](https://github.com/CambridgeCentreForProteomics/f1000_subcellular_dia_extension). 

The result of such a database search is a list of 
**peptide spectrum matches (PSMs), or precursors**, that is a list of matches between observed and expected
spectra. Most software will also aggregate the PSM or precursor level data
upward and provide output files at all data levels (PSM/precursor, peptide and protein).
It is up to the user which output file to use for further analysis.

The starting point for this workshop and data processing workflow in R is an 
output file from the identification search. Different softwares output different
file formats, for example the Proteome Discoverer v3.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific)
outputs a `.txt` file format, as does [MaxQuant](https://www.maxquant.org), 
[FragPipe](https://fragpipe.nesvilab.org), other such as [DIA-NN](https://github.com/vdemichev/DiaNN) output
parquet formats, will will show in the subsequent section how to import such
data. Of note, the data was reprocessed using DIA-NN v2.0 (Academia) meaning that
the files are no longer the exact ones used by [@Kieran2025].
:::

## Which data level should you start from?

Proteomics search and quantification software can report results at several
levels: PSMs, precursors (a peptide sequence with its modifications and charge
state), modified peptides, peptide sequences, and protein groups. In general, we
recommend starting from the lowest level available. This gives you maximum
control over data quality filtering, normalisation and aggregation, and makes
each step of the analysis easier to understand and report transparently.

What "lowest level" means depends on the acquisition method. For TMT data
acquired by DDA, each MS2 spectrum is matched to a peptide, so analysis can
start from the PSM level. In DIA, MS2 spectra are chimeric and identification is
peptide-centric, so there are no PSMs and the lowest level is the precursor.
Some tools for label-free data also only accept peptide-level input, so starting
at the lowest level is not always possible.

The data we will use in this workshop is label-free DIA-LOP, so we will start
from the precursor level (rather than the PSM-level TMT data typical of DDA
LOPIT). The data was reprocessed using DIA-NN v2.0 (Academia) meaning that the
files are no longer the exact ones used by [@Kieran2025].

## Summary
The use-case data that we will process and analyse in this workshop is a **DIA**
**label-free** **LOP** subcellular proteomics dataset on human U-2 OS cells. The aim of the experiment is
to determine **where proteins reside in the cell** (their subcellular
localisation).
